passage: Thursday night. Dear Diary, Kamal here. Today I gave Rukmini a note. It said, "Thank you for sharing your tiffin when I forgot mine. You are my best friend." I couldn't say it in her face, my mouth got stuck. She read it in the corridor and put it in her pencil box, and didn't say anything, but she smiled all the way to class. Chhoti Didi tried to read this diary earlier, so I hid it behind my school shoes. I don't like it when people read my diary. I will keep writing here. Tomorrow I'll write a thank-you letter to Nani too. 🙂

qa.q: What did Kamal write in the note to Rukmini?
qa.a: Kamal wrote, "Thank you for sharing your tiffin when I forgot mine. You are my best friend."

qa.q: Why did Kamal write the note instead of saying it to Rukmini?
qa.a: Kamal felt their mouth got stuck, so writing was easier for a feeling that was hard to say aloud. Kamal may also have felt shy about Rukmini's reaction.

qa.q: What could Kamal do about Chhoti Didi trying to read the diary?
qa.a: Kamal could tell Chhoti Didi calmly that the diary is private, or ask a parent to help set a rule about respecting each other's diaries.

qa.q: How does Rukmini feel about the note?
qa.a: Rukmini says nothing but smiles all the way to class and keeps the note in her pencil box, so she seems touched, though she may be shy too.

grounding: A child writes a thank-you note and a diary to share feelings hard to say aloud, and wants the diary's privacy respected.

passage: Zeenat sat on the charpai under the mango tree with a pencil and a torn page. Her friend Dilnaz was going away to her uncle's town for the whole summer, and Zeenat didn't know what to say. She wrote: "Dear Dilnaz, I will miss playing kho-kho with you. Please write to me." Then she crossed out "miss" and wrote "really miss". She folded it small and tucked it into Dilnaz's school bag while she wasn't looking. Later she saw Dilnaz pull it out on the bullock cart, read it twice, and press it to her chest. Zeenat looked away and pretended to count the coconut trees. ❤️

qa.q: Where did Zeenat sit while writing the letter?
qa.a: She sat on the charpai under the mango tree.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she crossed out "miss" and wrote "really miss", and what else might explain her looking away later?
qa.a: She felt sad about the separation and wanted her feelings to show clearly on paper. She looked away perhaps because she was shy watching Dilnaz read something so personal.

qa.q: What could Zeenat and Dilnaz do to keep their friendship going over the summer?
qa.a: They could write letters to each other, share small news from their days, and plan a game to play when Dilnaz returns.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when she reads the letter on the bullock cart?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and cared for, since she reads it twice and presses it to her chest, though she might also feel sad about leaving.

grounding: A school-age child writes a note to a friend, sharing feelings that are hard to say aloud.

passage:
In Oslo, Jin sat at the kitchen table chewing her pencil. At school she had shouted at her friend Astrid for snapping her favourite blue crayon, and Astrid had walked away without a word. Now Jin's stomach felt knotted, but every time she practised saying sorry out loud, her throat closed up.
So she took a pink card and wrote: "Sorry I yelled. It was only a crayon. I miss drawing with you. Friends again?"
She drew a tiny broken crayon with a plaster on it.
The next morning she slipped the card into Astrid's pencil case and hurried to her seat.
At lunch Astrid found it, read it twice, and wrote underneath: "Friends! I'll bring my crayons tomorrow 🙂"
Jin read the reply under the desk and grinned all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Jin draw on the card?
qa.a: A tiny broken crayon with a plaster on it.

qa.q: Why did Jin write the apology instead of saying it?
qa.a: Jin felt guilty and embarrassed, and every time she tried to say sorry aloud her throat closed up, so writing was easier than speaking.

qa.q: What made Jin's note work well?
qa.a: It was short and honest: it owned the yelling, said the crayon mattered less than the friendship, and asked a simple question Astrid could answer.

qa.q: How might Astrid have felt walking away and then finding the card?
qa.a: Astrid was probably hurt when she walked away, and the card likely made her feel relieved and cared for, so replying in writing felt easy.

grounding: A child writes a note to say sorry because the feeling is hard to say aloud, and her friend replies in writing.

passage:
Every night at the girls' hostel, Rashmi wrote in her green diary: about missing Amma's rasam, her little brother's silly jokes, and the heavy feeling after lights out.
One evening she left it open on her bed and went to brush her teeth.
Her roommate Charu came in, saw the open page, and stopped. Her eyes caught the first line. Then she closed the diary and put it back on the pillow.
When Rashmi returned, Charu said, "Your diary was open. I shut it. I read one line by mistake, sorry."
Rashmi's face went red. "Which line?"
"Just 'Dear diary.' Honestly."
Rashmi let out a breath. "Thanks. It's... private."
"I keep one too," Charu said. "Under my mattress."
After that they talked about home sometimes, but never about each other's diaries.

qa.q: Where does Charu keep her own diary?
qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she asked "Which line?"
qa.a: Rashmi felt embarrassed and anxious that her private feelings about home had been read, and then relieved when Charu said it was only "Dear diary".

qa.q: What did Charu do well?
qa.a: She shut the diary instead of reading on, and told Rashmi honestly, which respected Rashmi's privacy and kept her trust.

qa.q: How might the friendship have changed if Charu had read the whole diary?
qa.a: Rashmi might have felt exposed and stopped writing freely, and she might not have trusted Charu enough to talk about home later.

grounding: A hostel child uses a diary for feelings that are hard to say aloud, and a roommate respects its privacy.

passage:
For a whole week I noticed Francis writing on a small card at the back of the school bus, covering it with his arm whenever someone leaned over. He hardly ever speaks in class, so I was curious.
On Friday, as we got off, he handed the card to our bus driver, Mr Kamal, and ran. Mr Kamal read it right there on the step. He smiled, folded it carefully, and put it in his shirt pocket.
At the gate I asked Francis what it said. He shrugged. "Just thanks. For waiting when I'm late."
I never knew Francis noticed things like that.
The next Monday Mr Kamal gave Francis a thumbs-up from his seat, and Francis gave a tiny wave back.
- Salma

qa.q: Where did Mr Kamal put the card?
qa.a: He folded it carefully and put it in his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What might Francis have been feeling while writing the card, and what is another reading of covering it?
qa.a: Francis probably felt grateful but shy, since he covered the card and ran after giving it; covering it might also just mean he wanted it to be a surprise.

qa.q: What would you advise Salma if Salma wants to get to know Francis?
qa.a: Salma could chat with him gently about small things, or even pass a note, since Francis seems more comfortable writing than speaking.

qa.q: How does Mr Kamal seem to see the card?
qa.a: He seems touched and pleased, reading it at once, keeping it safely, and later greeting Francis with a thumbs-up.

grounding: A classmate observes a quiet child writing a thank-you card, showing writing helps share feelings that are hard to say aloud.

passage:
Monday: Nilesh couldn't get the words out when Kamal bhaiya fixed his broken cycle chain, so he left a note on Kamal's pillow: "Thank you. You are the best mechanic in Pune."
Wednesday: After a bad day at the new school, Nilesh wrote in his diary: "Nobody sat with me at lunch." Kamal found the diary on the sofa and started to open it. Mummy took it gently from his hand. "That's Nilesh's. We don't read it unless he asks." Kamal put it back, embarrassed.
Friday: Nilesh slipped a note under Kamal's door: "Thanks for not reading my diary. School is hard. Nobody sits with me." Kamal wrote back: "Want me to walk you in tomorrow?" Nilesh underlined "Yes" twice.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's thank-you note call Kamal?
qa.a: The best mechanic in Pune.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh leave a note instead of saying thank you aloud?
qa.a: Nilesh felt grateful but too shy to get the words out, so writing let the feeling through.

qa.q: Which choice made it safe for Nilesh to share his school worries?
qa.a: Respecting the diary's privacy; because it wasn't read, Nilesh chose to tell Kamal in a note, on his own terms.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt when Mummy took the diary from his hand?
qa.a: Kamal felt embarrassed, but putting it back earned trust, and two days later Nilesh shared the worry with him directly.

grounding: It illustrates a child using notes and a diary to share feelings that are hard to say aloud, and a family respecting the diary's privacy.
